paper_style.palette_strategy: 理论图主要使用 black/gray 与 node shape/line-style redundancy；Figure 2、Figure 7、Figure 8 使用局部 categorical palette，颜色语义在对象内稳定但没有全局 palette 或统一 legend。
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: pdfimages -list 对 48 页无嵌入位图 XObject；8 个 Figure 和 5 个 Table 均以 PDF vector/text 观察，Figure 7 的曲线与 bands、Figure 8 的网络边、Table 3 的 CDF microplots 也为向量路径。
paper_style.style_consistency: 正文/理论对象保持 serif 数学论文风格，图表整体使用 booktabs/minimal rules；理论网络之间的黑白 shape/line grammar 一致，但统计 Figure 7、彩色 Figure 8 的字体与 palette 不完全统一，且灰度鲁棒性不一致。

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Examples of reducing models to their irreducible forms via the procedure in Proposition 2. Throughout, white circles denote observed variables and grey squares denote latent variables.

color.semantic_mapping: Black edges/labels and boxes; gray filled squares are latent variables; white circles are observed variables.

encodings.x: Left-to-right reduction sequence within each example.
encodings.y: Node placement only; no quantitative y variable.
encodings.shape: Square latent nodes versus circular observed nodes.
encodings.line: Solid directed causal arrows; the word reduce labels the operation.
encodings.facet: Four reduction examples placed in one horizontal row.
encodings.text: L_i/X_i node labels, reduce, and panel-local graph notation.

figures.data_and_statistics: No numerical data are plotted. The four examples show removing non-ancestors and reducing maximal redundant latent sets until an irreducible representative remains.
figures.evidence_relation: Definition 2 and Proposition 1–2 establish the irreducible boundary; Figure 1 gives concrete reduction cases before the irreducible input assumed by glvLiNG in §5.
design_strengths: Four examples make before/after graph changes directly traceable.
Node shape and fill redundantly encode latent/observed status.
The restrained black/gray grammar keeps the theoretical operation prominent.
design_weaknesses: Panels lack local labels explaining which specific reduction rule fires.
The caption defines node types but not the maximal redundant-latent criterion.
Small arrows and labels become difficult to inspect after page reduction.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a repeated node-shape grammar for original-to-reduced graph transformations; annotate each panel with the exact local rule when reusing the pattern.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: An illustration of path ranks, edge ranks, and their duality. Left: a digraph G with vertices V partitioned to Y, C, and Z, shown by different colors. The path rank ρ_G (Z, Y) = 2, with C being a min-cut. Right: the dual edge rank r_G (V \ Y, V \ Z) = 4, given by the maximum bipartite matching from V \ Z to V \ Y, i.e., from Y ∪ C to Z ∪ C, with four matched edges highlighted in red. Four corresponding nonzero entries placed on diagonal, also in red, confirm mrank(Q^(G)_{V\Y, V\Z}) = 4. One may examine the duality in Theorem 1: w.l.o.g. let m ≤ n, there is m − 2 = m + n + 2 − n − 4.

color.semantic_mapping: Orange, pink, and lavender partition vertices into Y/C/Z; red highlights the four matching edges and corresponding matrix entries; black is structure and text.

encodings.x: No metric x axis; left/right regions correspond to graph, matching and matrix representations.
encodings.y: No metric y axis; node/matrix row placement carries set membership.
encodings.color: Y/C/Z set membership and red correspondence highlight.
encodings.shape: Circular graph vertices and matrix cells/entries; matching is represented by directed edges.
encodings.line: Solid directed graph/matching arrows; red overlay marks matched edges.
encodings.facet: Two coordinated views: path-rank bottleneck on the left and dual edge-rank matching/support matrix on the right.
encodings.text: Y_i, C_i, Z_i labels; ρ_G, r_G and matrix rank/matching notation.

figures.data_and_statistics: This is a constructed theoretical example, not a sample summary. The left graph has ρ_G(Z,Y)=2 with C as a min-cut; the right view has r_G(V\Y,V\Z)=4, four red matching edges and four red diagonal nonzero support entries.
figures.evidence_relation: Path-rank constraints in §3.1 motivate the bottleneck view; Figure 2 instantiates Theorem 1 duality, which is then rewritten as the local edge-rank criterion in Lemma 5 and Theorem 2.
design_strengths: Graph, bipartite matching and matrix encodings are aligned in one object.
Red one-to-one highlights make the duality auditable rather than purely verbal.
Set labels and formulas supply semantic redundancy for the pastel fills.
design_weaknesses: Dense matrix indices and the final m−2 equality require backtracking to the theorem.
The pastel Y/C/Z palette loses separation in grayscale or projection.
The figure does not state the practical locality benefit of edge ranks.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show one theoretical quantity through graph, combinatorial and algebraic views, reusing matched color/highlight tokens to establish correspondence.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: An example distributional equivalence class consisting of 6 digraphs up to L-relabeling.

color.semantic_mapping: Black graph nodes/edges and text; gray antialiasing; white panel background. Operation class is encoded by solid versus dashed connectors rather than hue.

encodings.x: Horizontal progression across G1→G3 and G4→G6; not a numerical axis.
encodings.y: Two cycle-reversal configurations arranged in rows; not a numerical axis.
encodings.color: No substantive color variable; grayscale ink.
encodings.shape: Square latent and circular observed nodes inside six boxed graph panels.
encodings.line: Solid arrows inside graphs and between states for edge +/-; dashed vertical arrows for cycle reversal.
encodings.text: G1…G6, L1/L2, X1/X2/X3, Edge +/− and Cycle reversal.

figures.data_and_statistics: No numerical data or aggregation. Each boxed panel is one irreducible digraph; connectors encode admissible edge additions/deletions and cycle reversal, up to latent relabeling.
figures.evidence_relation: Lemmas 6–7 define the admissible operations; Figure 3 visualizes the six-state example used immediately in Example 2 and motivates Theorem 3 and BFS/DFS class traversal.
design_strengths: The state-panel layout makes class membership and two operation families visible together.
Solid/dashed connector redundancy survives grayscale.
Six states are small enough for manual edge-level checking.
design_weaknesses: Connector labels do not name the particular edge being added or deleted.
The L-relabeling qualification is only in the caption.
Dense node labels and arrows are small at normal page scale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Represent an equivalence class as state panels joined by typed operation edges; add edge tokens beside connectors when applying it to a larger class.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Example Hasse diagrams (defined in Lemma 12) over the solution sets of matroid-preserving column augmentations. Instances from the earlier Example 3 are used. In each diagram, the root vertices, corresponding to the minimal solutions (see Corollary 2) are highlighted in red, while the leaf vertex, corresponding to the unique maximal solution (see Corollary 1) are highlighted in blue.

color.semantic_mapping: Red roots mark minimal solutions; blue leaves mark the unique maximal solution; black nodes/edges are intermediate solutions and covers.

encodings.x: No metric x axis; three augmentation instances are placed left-to-right.
encodings.y: Set inclusion/Hasse level from minimal to maximal solution, not a metric axis.
encodings.shape: Filled circular vertices carrying set labels.
encodings.line: Solid directed cover arrows in each Hasse diagram.
encodings.facet: Three side-by-side panels α, β, γ.
encodings.text: Set-valued node labels and G^aug_{Q,α/β/γ} panel labels.

figures.data_and_statistics: No uncertainty or sampled data. Nodes are all shown solutions in three small matroid-preserving column-augmentation examples; arrows represent one-element Hasse covers, with minimal roots and unique maximal leaves highlighted.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix B constructs single-column augmentations; Lemma 12 proves weak connectivity; Figure 4 is the finite solution-set visual used before the multiple-column decomposition and Theorem 3.
design_strengths: Set labels make each solution vertex inspectable.
Red/blue endpoint marking exposes the two theoretical boundary results.
The same Hasse grammar is repeated for three examples.
design_weaknesses: Red/blue status is not reliably distinguishable in grayscale.
The caption does not define that arrows are exact Hasse covers.
The earlier Example 3 inputs are outside the figure, so the panels are not standalone.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a Hasse diagram to replace a long solution list while marking minimal and maximal boundaries; add a small legend and explicit cover semantics in a new use.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: Left: An example distributional equivalence class consisting of 10 digraphs. Right: Transitions among these digraphs, where solid edges indicate edge additions or deletions, and dashed edges indicate cycle reversals.

color.semantic_mapping: Black/gray directed graph ink; white panel background; operation family is carried by solid/dashed transition lines.

encodings.x: Left grid enumerates G1…G10; right transition layout is categorical, not metric.
encodings.y: Left rows group graph panels; right vertical arrangement groups transition states.
encodings.color: No substantive color variable; grayscale network ink.
encodings.shape: Square latent and circular observed nodes; graph panels and transition nodes provide grouping.
encodings.line: Solid directed graph/transition edges for edge addition/deletion; dashed transition edges for cycle reversal.
encodings.facet: Left 3×3 state grid plus right transition graph.
encodings.text: G1…G10 and L1/X1/X2/X3 labels; caption defines line semantics.

figures.data_and_statistics: No numerical sample statistic. The left side enumerates ten digraphs; the right side gives their transition graph. The text after the figure states that the solid-only components have 3, 3 and 4 digraphs and illustrates intersecting cycles.
figures.evidence_relation: Extends the six-state Figure 3 example in Appendix C.2; tests Theorem 3 in a class where cycle-reversal components need not be isomorphic, then feeds the CP(G) examples in Figure 6.
design_strengths: State enumeration and transition topology are shown side-by-side.
Line style directly distinguishes the two admissible operation families.
The same graph grammar as the main-text example supports visual continuity.
design_weaknesses: Ten small digraphs make individual arrows hard to verify.
The transition graph does not label which edge changed on each link.
Component sizes and the intersecting-cycle finding are in surrounding prose rather than the object.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair representative graph states with a typed transition graph when an equivalence class has multiple transformation components; label component sizes for immediate comparison.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Illustrative presentations of equivalence classes. Left: Presentation of equivalent digraphs G1, G2, G3 under a same cycle-reversal configuration from Figure 3. The basis digraph shown is the unique maximal equivalent digraph (Step 2 above). In it, solid edges denote those that must appear in all equivalent digraphs, while dashed edges are those that can be removed (Step 3 above). One may use Corollaries 1 and 2 to check how they are determined. Right: A similar presentation for digraphs G3, G4, G7, G10 from Figure 5. Remark: One might ask why we present the equivalence class separately for each cycle-reversal configuration rather than for the entire class. The reason is that taking the union over all digraphs in the entire class can, unlike within one configuration, yield a supergraph that is itself out of the equivalence class, potentially producing misleading interpretations. In fact, this separation only leads to more informative presentations, shown by Theorem 4 below.

color.semantic_mapping: Black solid/dashed directed edges and node outlines; gray antialiasing; edge type, not hue, carries must/may status.

encodings.x: No metric x axis; left and right are two CP(G) configurations.
encodings.y: No metric y axis; node layout only.
encodings.color: No substantive color variable; all semantics are shape/line based.
encodings.shape: Square latent and circular observed nodes.
encodings.line: Solid directed edges are must-appear; dashed directed edges are removable in at least one equivalent graph.
encodings.facet: Two side-by-side presentations for separate cycle-reversal configurations.
encodings.text: L/X node labels and context supplied by caption.

figures.data_and_statistics: No numerical data. Each side is a maximal basis digraph with solid invariant edges and dashed edges that can be removed in some equivalent graph; dashed edges remain jointly constrained by rank conditions.
figures.evidence_relation: Theorem 4 and Appendix C.3 Steps 1–3 define CP(G); Figure 6 links the maximal graph and must-appear edge construction to the earlier class examples and to possible experimental-design interpretation.
design_strengths: Maximal basis, invariant edges and variable edges are compressed into one graph.
Solid/dashed encoding remains readable without color.
The caption explains why configurations are shown separately rather than unioned.
design_weaknesses: Dashed does not mean arbitrarily removable, but that caveat is not repeated adjacent to the figure.
Different layouts make edge-count comparison across sides difficult.
Class size and the set of constraints are not quantified in the graphic.
figures.reusable_pattern: Present structural uncertainty as a maximal graph with solid invariant and dashed optional edges, while stating that optional edges remain subject to global constraints.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7: Simulation results comparing glvLiNG with existing methods with varying sample size N (the global x-axis), and each subplot shows a setting under a specific number of total variables n, number of latent variables ℓ, and the average in-degree d. Mean and standard deviation of SHD are calculated from 25 random irreducible models.

color.semantic_mapping: Blue/orange/green lines identify glvLiNG, LaHiCaSl and PO-LiNGAM; corresponding translucent tints are standard-deviation bands.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: top center, shared across all panels

encodings.x: Sample size N, shared log scale with ticks around 10^3, 10^4 and 10^5.
encodings.y: SHD (mean±std), linear within each row; lower is better.
encodings.color: Method identity and matching uncertainty band.
encodings.shape: Small point markers on each method curve; no method-specific shape.
encodings.line: Three solid method curves; translucent bands show ± standard deviation.
encodings.facet: Columns vary latent count ℓ and average in-degree d; rows vary total vertices n; 24 feasible panels are populated.
encodings.text: Shared legend, per-panel ℓ/d headers, right-side n labels, global SHD and Sample size N labels.

figures.data_and_statistics: Finite-sample simulation means and standard deviations of SHD over 25 random irreducible models per panel. N ranges from 1,000 to 200,000; n is 5–13, ℓ is 1–5 where feasible, and d is 1 or 3. Sparse d=1 panels often favor baselines, while dense d=3 panels generally show lower glvLiNG curves; the paper also reports n=13,d=3 latent-robustness values in surrounding text.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix D.4 fixes the ER generation, weights/noise and equivalence-class SHD definition; Figure 7 is the finite-sample counterpart to the oracle baseline Table 5 and the dense/sparse claims in §5.
design_strengths: A regular small-multiple grid exposes interactions among n, ℓ, d and N.
Shared legend and global log x-axis reduce repeated furniture.
Mean lines and SD bands show both trend and variability.
design_weaknesses: Blank infeasible cells are not explained in the graphic.
Per-row y ranges make absolute cross-row heights incomparable.
All three methods use the same solid line/marker grammar, so grayscale comparison is weak.
Caption omits the color mapping and the lower-is-better direction.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a feasible-combination small-multiple grid for multi-factor simulation, with a shared log sample axis and uncertainty bands; add redundant line styles and explicit empty-cell semantics in a new version.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.module: Appendix D.5; Hong Kong stock-market dataset

caption.text: Figure 8: Presentation of the equivalence class that glvLiNG estimates from the stock market data. Different colors of nodes indicate different sectors. Solid and dashed edges indicate edges that must appear in all or at least one equivalent graph(s).

color.semantic_mapping: Node fills distinguish sectors (banking/real estate/utilities/commerce) and gray latent nodes; solid/dashed edge styles carry must/may status.

encodings.x: Graph-layout x position only; no geographic or temporal x variable.
encodings.y: Graph-layout y position only; no quantitative y variable.
encodings.shape: Ellipses for observed stocks and squares for latent variables.
encodings.line: Solid directed edges must appear in all equivalent graphs; dashed edges appear in at least one equivalent graph.
encodings.text: Node number and stock-name labels, L1/L2 latent labels, and directed arrowheads.

figures.data_and_statistics: The real-world input has 14 Hong Kong stocks and 1,331 daily samples (2000-01-04–2005-06-17). glvLiNG estimates a class of 19,008 graphs over 14+2 vertices with 29–34 edges; the presentation shows 20 solid and 14 dashed edges. Node color is sector, not a numerical measurement.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix D.5 maps the glvLiNG output and Theorem 4 CP(G) presentation to domain observations: large banks upstream, real-estate receivers, utility-heavy cycles, and one interpretable latent parent of three stocks.
design_strengths: Solid/dashed edges combine causal direction and equivalence uncertainty.
Node labels, shape and color provide multiple ways to identify latent versus observed variables.
The domain network makes the theoretical presentation concrete.
design_weaknesses: Dense curved edges cross and require slow tracing.
No separate sector legend; pale fills are projection/grayscale fragile.
Layout position has no domain spatial meaning but this is not stated in the caption.
The 19,008-member class and edge range are only in surrounding prose.
figures.reusable_pattern: Apply maximal-graph plus invariant/optional-edge encoding to a domain network, retaining labels and a sector palette; provide a legend or expandable edge list when density grows.

tables.label: Table 1
tables.module: Appendix C.1; summary of path ranks and edge ranks

caption.text: Table 1: A side-by-side comparison between path ranks and edge ranks.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty; symbolic definitions and identities only.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five aspect rows align intuition, full-rank matrix condition, graphical constraint, matroid representation and Theorem 1 duality. Cells use equations and citations rather than numerical precision.
tables.evidence_relation: §3.1–§3.3 definitions and Theorem 1 are compressed into an appendix bridge table; it prepares the local edge-rank formulation used by Theorem 2.
design_strengths: Symmetric columns make algebraic and combinatorial viewpoints easy to compare row by row.
The final duality row preserves the central equality.
Booktabs rules and whitespace keep the symbolic table legible.
design_weaknesses: Long equations wrap inside narrow columns.
The caption does not state why edge rank is operationally local.
The table is not self-contained without the definitions cited in cells.
tables.reusable_pattern: Arrange a theoretical bridge as aspect rows that progress intuition→formula→graph→matroid→duality.

tables.label: Table 2
tables.module: Appendix C.5; related-work equivalence characterization overview

caption.text: Table 2: A side-by-side overview of representative works on equivalence characterizations across different settings using different approaches. The final column summarizes this work’s contributions.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty or numeric precision; citations and theorem labels are textual references.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five comparison rows cover Structural Level 1–3, Transformational and Traversal algorithms. The columns compare fully observed acyclic graphs, acyclic latent graphs and this work’s latent cyclic LiNG setting; a category multirow column groups Structural/Transformational/Traversal.
tables.evidence_relation: Table 2 positions Theorems 1–4 against classical Markov/latent equivalence and traversal work; it is literature evidence rather than an empirical result.
design_strengths: The final column puts this work’s contribution on the same row as prior settings.
Multirow category labels expose the structural/transformational/traversal taxonomy.
Coverage includes both characterization and class traversal.
design_weaknesses: Dense citations and long prose make row heights uneven.
Level meanings and abbreviations are not defined in the caption.
Cell content is difficult to scan without reading Appendix C.5 prose.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use setting columns and capability rows to map a theory contribution against prior equivalence regimes, reserving a final column for the new result.

tables.label: Table 3
tables.module: Appendix D.1; exhaustive graph and equivalence-class enumeration

caption.text: Table 3: For different numbers of vertices n and latent vertices ℓ, we report the total number of weakly connected digraphs with n vertices, the subset that are irreducible when the first ℓ vertices are latent (both with and without L-isomorphic variants), and the corresponding numbers of distributional equivalence classes they fall into. The final two columns present statistics on how irreducible digraphs (both with and without L-isomorphic variants) are distributed among those equivalence classes.

tables.uncertainty: No mean±SD or confidence interval; the final two columns show empirical CDFs of class-size distributions.
tables.data_and_statistics: Four n groups (3–6) and 14 n–ℓ rows report all weakly connected digraphs, irreducible counts with/without L-isomorphic variants, unique-up-to-L-relabeling counts, and class counts. The two rightmost columns contain one CDF pair per condition, with x=log10(#digraphs per class) and y=CDF.
tables.evidence_relation: D.1 quantifies the search space that Figures 3/5 illustrate and explains why traversal limits matter; exact enumeration counts are not a performance estimate.
design_strengths: Combines exact counts with distribution shape instead of reporting only an average class size.
Separates L-isomorphic variants from unique-up-to-relabeling counts.
The CDF panels expose class-size heterogeneity.
design_weaknesses: Rotated page-width layout and many microplots are difficult to read.
Row-to-CDF alignment is visually demanding.
CDF normalization and L-isomorphic terminology require surrounding prose.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair exact enumeration columns with per-condition distribution microplots, but split a rotated composite into readable panels for reuse.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4: Running time comparison between our glvLiNG algorithm and a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) baseline for constructing digraphs that satisfy the rank constraints of oracle OICA mixing matrices. Ground-truth graphs are generated from the Erdős–Rényi model with total number of vertices n and average in-degree avgdeg, with ℓ vertices randomly designated as latent. Each entry reports the mean and standard deviation over 50 models (when completed); empty entries indicate runs that did not finish within 10 minutes. All times are reported in seconds. Experiments were run on an Apple M4 chip.

tables.uncertainty: Each numeric entry is mean ± standard deviation over 50 models when completed; blank MILP entries mean timeout at 10 minutes, not zero.
tables.data_and_statistics: Rows span n=5,7,9,11,13, latent count ℓ and avgdeg 1/3. Columns report seconds for MILP, total glvLiNG, glvLiNG Phase 1 and Phase 2; values use three decimal places.
tables.evidence_relation: The rank-realization complexity claim in §5 is split into total/phase costs here; blank timeout cells expose the baseline failure boundary rather than hiding it.
design_strengths: End-to-end, phase decomposition, baseline, hardware and unit are in one table.
Mean±SD and repetition count are explicit.
Timeout semantics are stated in the caption and preserved as blank cells.
design_weaknesses: No explicit speedup or timeout-status column; comparisons require mental arithmetic.
Nested row groups leave substantial white space.
Three decimal places make near-zero Phase 2 differences look more exact than they are.
tables.reusable_pattern: Report total and phase costs with explicit timeout semantics, units, hardware and repetitions; add a speedup/status column when space permits.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: Evaluation of existing methods under possible model misspecification on arbitrary latent-variable models. Ground-truth graphs are generated from the Erdős–Rényi model with total number of vertices n and average in-degree avgdeg, with ℓ vertices randomly designated as latent. Only irreducible models are chosen. Each entry reports the mean and standard deviation of the structural Hamming distances (SHDs) between the result and truth over 50 random models. Algorithms are provided with their oracle tests, that is, for them to directly query oracle generalized independent noise (GIN) conditions from the digraph. When the number of their identified latent variables is fewer than truth, we simply add isolated latent variables into the result. When the identified number of latents is larger (which seems not happened), we planned to choose the removal that leads to best result. Finally, the best possible result is reported, i.e., we choose the digraph in the ground-truth equivalence class that is closer to their output as the truth. The latent variables are viewed as unlabeled.

tables.uncertainty: Each PO-LiNGAM/LaHiCaSl cell reports SHD mean ± SD over 50 random irreducible models; no confidence intervals or significance marks.
tables.data_and_statistics: Rows vary n=10,15,20, ℓ and avgdeg=1–4; columns are n, ℓ, avgdeg, PO-LiNGAM and LaHiCaSl. Values use two decimal places. Latents are unlabeled and the truth is chosen as the closest graph in the ground-truth equivalence class.
tables.evidence_relation: The table isolates model misspecification under oracle GIN inputs, complementing Figure 7’s finite-sample comparison and the structural-assumption discussion in §5.
design_strengths: Oracle protocol and equivalence-class truth comparison are defined in the caption.
Coverage spans graph size, latent count and density.
Mean±SD and fixed 50-model repetition make rows comparable.
design_weaknesses: glvLiNG is absent because this table targets existing methods under oracle inputs.
No column reports latent-count mismatch or failure rate.
The closest-in-class truth convention makes SHD interpretation non-obvious despite the long caption.
tables.reusable_pattern: Under fixed oracle inputs, stratify structural misspecification by n, latent count and density and report SHD mean±SD with a clearly defined truth space.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Model reduction (Figure 1) leads to path/edge-rank bridge (Figure 2/Table 1), equivalence-class transformations (Figure 3/Figure 5), augmentation proof traversal (Figure 4), CP(G) presentation (Figure 6), then enumeration/runtime/oracle evidence (Tables 3–5), finite-sample simulation (Figure 7) and stock-market presentation (Figure 8).
cross_object_system.caption_system: Captions use regular Figure/Table k prefixes and usually move from title to setup/encoding; Figure 6, Figure 7 and Tables 4–5 provide the strongest semantic definitions, while short theory captions rely on the surrounding theorem text. Main-finding sentences are uncommon except in Figure 6/Table 2 wording.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Tables use serif/math fonts, bold or medium headers and booktabs/minimal horizontal rules. Concept tables use prose/formula columns; experiment tables use structural condition columns followed by method/cost columns, with row groups carried by multirow labels and blank cells.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: There is no dedicated ablation Figure; Figure 1–6 make method/theory interfaces explicit, Tables 4–5 isolate efficiency and structural misspecification, and Figure 7 compares finite-sample outcomes. Table 3 supplies search-space scale rather than an ablation.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main Figures 1–3 introduce irreducibility, rank duality and transformations; Appendix Figures 4–6 expand proofs and presentation, Tables 1–5 supply theory/related-work/enumeration/runtime/oracle details, and Figures 7–8 close the simulation and real-data links referenced in §5.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern dominate body, captions and theory diagrams; Figure 7 uses TeX Gyre Termes/Heros and NewTX math, and Figure 8 exposes Times New Roman/Type3 graph labels. The serif/math register is consistent, but exact font families and sizes are not globally locked.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Black/gray is the stable theoretical default with shape and line-style redundancy. Figure 2 pastel set colors, Figure 7 method colors/bands and Figure 8 sector fills are locally coherent but use different palettes; Figure 7 and Figure 8 are not reliably grayscale-safe.

most_reusable_patterns: Maximal graph plus solid invariant/dashed optional edges (Figure 6) to summarize equivalence-class uncertainty.
Graph–matching–matrix coordinated views with shared highlights (Figure 2) to explain a theoretical duality.
Feasible-factor small multiples with a shared log axis and uncertainty bands (Figure 7).
Runtime tables that retain total/phase cost, repetition statistics and explicit timeout semantics (Table 4).
highest_value_objects: Figure 6: CP(G) turns Theorem 4 into an interpretable relation summary.
Figure 2: the path-rank/edge-rank/matrix correspondence is the clearest theory bridge.
Figure 7: the only dense empirical curve object, exposing density and latent-dimension interactions.
Table 4: end-to-end efficiency and failure boundary are visible in one evidence surface.
failure_patterns: Several short captions identify an object but omit the main conclusion and denominator/operation details.
Pastel colors and same-style colored curves lose information in grayscale; Figure 7 lacks line-style redundancy.
